first.rationale: Two observed declines (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) are internal, addressable, and directly matched by two inherited memories (memory_86 on shortening onboarding, memory_31 on signup simplification). Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the reflexive answer to the competitor's entry pricing, but discount-led SMB acquisition is the classic path to unqualified, churn-prone revenue, which conflicts with the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue; it also cedes pricing ground that is hard to reclaim. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) and referrals (memory_57) address neither current decline. I am spending the single verification pull on memory_31 rather than on the option I am rejecting, because memory_31 is the weakest link in the plan I actually intend to run: it is the oldest record (day 12), and 'cutting required fields at signup' is exactly the kind of intervention whose consolidated summary ('durable lift in first-week activation') can survive while the caveat that looser signup gates admit lower-intent accounts is stripped out. The archived record should show whether the original experiment tracked anything downstream of activation — lead quality, paid conversion, retention — or only the top-of-funnel metric. Important caveat: all six memories are consolidated summaries, not primary evidence, and they were measured in a pre-competitor environment; the current activation dip may be partly composition effect from the competitor skimming price-sensitive accounts rather than a pure funnel regression, in which case onboarding fixes will underdeliver. Therefore: small guarded test, not a broad rollout. Guardrails: hold out a control, gate on qualified-pipeline and 30/60-day retention rather than completion rate alone, and pre-commit to rollback if activation lift comes with a drop in downstream conversion quality. If memory_31 turns out to have measured only first-week activation with no downstream tracking, I will scope the test to memory_86's shortening/resequencing of onboarding for already-qualified signups and leave the signup field requirements intact.

final.rationale: The archive substantially confirms memory_31 but also vindicates the reason for checking it. The source record (exp_31: signup +15%, activation +9%, 30-day retention -1%, qualified revenue +4%) did track downstream metrics, and the direction survives on the objective that matters: qualified revenue is up, not just top-of-funnel. But two things the consolidated summary omitted are now visible. First, there is a real if small retention drag (-1%), consistent with looser signup gates admitting somewhat lower-intent accounts — the consolidated line 'durable lift in first-week activation' had that caveat stripped out. Second, the effect is explicitly scoped: 'Holds on SMB; not replicated on other segments.' Both facts narrow the action rather than reverse it. Decision: run simplify_onboarding, scoped to SMB self-serve only, as a small guarded test. This addresses the two internal declines actually observed (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) rather than chasing the competitor down a discount curve. Promotional pricing (memory_73) remains the tempting reflex given the competitor's entry pricing, but discount-led SMB acquisition trades directly against sustainable long-term qualified revenue and is hard to unwind once signalled; memory_73 also went unverified, so I am treating it as a consolidated summary of unknown fidelity rather than as evidence. Referral (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) address neither current decline. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving this week: exp_31 was run on day 12, in a pre-competitor market. Part of the current activation dip may be a composition effect — the competitor skimming price-sensitive accounts — rather than a funnel regression, in which case a funnel fix will underdeliver against the historical +9%. The -1% retention drag was also measured in that easier environment and could be larger now if the marginal signup is lower-intent. Guardrails, given the known drag: hold out a randomized control; gate success on qualified revenue and 30/60-day retention, not completion or activation rate alone; pre-register the -1% retention figure as the historical baseline and roll back if the test materially exceeds it; keep the change to SMB self-serve and do not extrapolate to other segments, which the source explicitly says did not replicate. Prefer memory_86's resequencing/shortening of the onboarding path over aggressive removal of signup fields where the two can be separated, since the retention cost is attributable to the looser gate rather than to the shorter path.
